title: What is known about 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it halts. Busycoq pull request 93 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-17) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. The right side is a sorted list of runs of 1s of lengths 13 + 6i, separated by 00, with fewer runs of each larger length: a counter in some mixed base, measured, not proved. The machine runs step for step like 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD--- (another batch) on the tape. Halting needs F on a 1, entered only from E on a 1; never one step away in the first 3·106 steps; the halt comes far later.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 37,151 cells have been visited and 22,314 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.503). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.162).

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: Lean proves, for every count and every tape around, the shift rules: D crosses (01)^n rightward turning it into (11)^n (2 steps per copy), and C crosses a run of 1s leftward (1 step per cell).

claims.title: A sorted list of runs 1^(13+6i)
claims.text: At the last right extension before 109 steps (step 948,962,681) the right part of the tape is 1,008 runs of 1s separated by 00: 616 runs 1^13, then 188 of 1^19, 121 of 1^25, 37 of 1^31, 22 of 1^37, 7 of 1^43, 4 of 1^49, and single runs 1^53, 1^59, 1^63, with a few short runs (7, 13, 17, 21, 27, 35, 40, 47) in between, which are the places being worked on. Left of it: (100)^3061 1^5 (001111111)^932 1100, the bouncer's region.

claims.title: Same tape as a machine in another batch
claims.text: 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD--- has the same triage numbers; sampled every 99,991 steps to 2·10<sup>6</sup>, and at 2·10<sup>8</sup>, the two machines have the same tape and number of 1s except at moments when the head is in the part where their tables differ (D1, E0).

claims.title: Never one step from a halt
claims.text: The machine halts when F reads a 1, and F is entered only from E reading a 1 (E1 → 0RF). In the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps E reads a 1 374,145 times, always with a 0 to its right.

claims.title: No halt in the first 6.63×10<sup>13</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 6.63×1013 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.00×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 7,849 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The list of runs behaves like a counter (each length 13 + 6i a digit, its multiplicity the digit's value, carries making longer runs), but the carry rule is not written down, let alone proved.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tape and head as 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD--- at every one of the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps (the tables differ). The same table as 1RB0LE_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_1LD0RF_0RA--- up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. The same table as 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC--- up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 1 other holdout (listed on the explainer page).

check: python3 holdouts/1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD---/py/rules.py && holdouts/1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD---/lean/check.sh      # regenerate and check the rules
python3 holdouts/1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LE_1LC0RF_0RD---/py/observe.py 1e7 B 6      # the tape at the last moments each end grew

explainer.lede: It halts. On the right of its tape it keeps a sorted list of runs of 1s whose lengths go up in steps of 6, fewer of each length than of the one before: a counter whose rows halve as they move up. Long after any simulation could follow, the counter's leftovers line up into the pattern that stops it: busycoq pull request 93 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind proves it in Rocq.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 37,151 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 1.00×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: A counter of digit rows, run by a proved engine
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 93 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch in about 9 minutes; it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions halt prints “Closed under the global context”). It does not find a formula for the run. It builds a fast simulator, the engine, proves in Coq that every step of the engine is a true statement about the machine, and then lets the engine run the machine from the blank tape until it halts.

A copy of the table. The proof first reflects the tape, so that left and right swap, and renames the states: this machine's A, B, C, D become C, D, A, B. That gives the table 1RB1RA_1LC0RE_1LD1LB_1RA0LE_1RA0LF_0LB--- started in state C. Coq checks transition by transition that the two runs are the same up to this change, so a halt of one is a halt of the other. From here on, directions and state names are those of that table. The same table started in states B and D is 1RB0LE_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_1LD0RF_0RA--- (pull request 82) and 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC--- (pull request 84, tape not reflected), both proved halting by the same kind of engine.

Digits and three moments. Write wn for the word w written n times. The proof's main word is the digit D n = 1 (11)n 00: a run of 2n+1 ones followed by two blanks. Call n its level. The runs of 13, 19, 25, … ones of the sections below are the digits D 6, D 9, D 12, seen reflected. Most of the tape is a long sequence of digits, mostly in rows of equal ones, the highest levels towards the left and the lowest at the right end. Near the left end, where the head turns, lie a few other kinds of word, among them blocks (10)b and (111)k. The proof watches the head at three kinds of moment: CfgR, state A at the word 0100, heading right over the digits; CfgL, state B heading left with a 1 just behind it; and CfgJ, state C heading left with 100 just behind it and a +1 to deliver.

Macro rules. About twenty rules say how the machine gets from one such moment to the next, for every level and every surrounding tape. Heading right, the head turns each digit D n it crosses into S n = 1 (01)n+1, a word of the same length. Heading left in CfgL it turns S n back into D n; in CfgJ it turns it into D (n+1), which is how a +1 is delivered. At the blank end of the tape the head writes two new digits D 0 and turns back. On the left, each 111 of a block (111)k is used up by one turn, so the block is a timer that allows k more round trips. And a round trip that finds two digits D 0 side by side merges them: 10 D0 D0 becomes D2 10, and the digit before them gets a +1; over a row, 2k digits D 0 become about k digits D 3. Rows of higher digits are merged in pairs in the same way, through a longer detour over the left part.

A counter. Together these rules make the digits a counter. Its places are the levels 0, 3, 6, …, and the number of digits in a row is the value at that place. Each pass halves a row and carries it one place up, while fresh digits D 0 keep arriving at the right end. This is binary counting with rows instead of bits, so a row of n digits lasts about log2 n passes. The halving is not exact: a row with an odd count leaves a digit over, and the proof has rules for these leftovers (it calls them defects). Where the leftovers end up depends on the parities of huge counts, and no formula for them is known. That is why the community calls such a machine a chaotic Bell.

The engine. The engine is a program written in Coq. It stores the tape compactly: the left part as a list of words with repeat counts, the digits as a list of pairs (level, how many in a row), all numbers in binary. In one engine step it looks at the tape near the head, picks the rule that applies, often a whole batch of them (k round trips at once, with k found by a division), and writes down the result. Where no rule fits, it makes single machine steps. One theorem, proved for every possible compact tape, says that each engine step is correct: the machine really goes from the tape before to the tape after, and when the engine reports a halt, the machine really halts.

How it stops. In this machine's own terms it halts only when state B reads a 1 and the two cells to its right are 1 too: B1 and E1 then put F on a 1. Nothing in the proof predicts when the leftovers will set this up; the engine simply runs until they do. Coq's virtual machine (vm_compute) evaluates the engine from the blank tape with a budget of 222 = 4,194,304 steps, and it stops after 2,452,242 of them, when the newest row holds about 10420 digits D 0, far beyond any direct simulation. So the computer checks one long but finite computation. What holds for all sizes (the rules, the batches, the correctness of every engine step) is proved by symbolic reasoning in Coq.

sections.heading: A sorted list of runs of 1s
html: At step 948,962,681 the right part of the tape is 1,008 runs of 1s separated by 0 0:

(1^13 is thirteen 1s.) The lengths go up by 6, the runs are sorted, and there are fewer of each length than of the one before. A handful of odd short runs mark places being worked on. On the left, (100)^3061 1^5 (001111111)^932 is the bouncer's region.

sections.heading: A counter made of runs
html: Read each length 13 + 6i as a digit place and its number of runs as the digit. As the machine runs, runs grow from one length to the next and new longer runs appear at the right end (longest 59 at step 7.6·108, 63 at 9.5·108), like carries. These are measurements; the carry rule is written down in the proof (see How the proof works).

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The machine stops only in F reading a 1, and F is entered only from E reading a 1 (moving right). In the first 3·106 steps E reads a 1 374,145 times and the next cell is always 0. It does happen later: after 2,452,242 steps of the proved engine of busycoq pull request 93, B reads 1 1 1 and E1 puts F on a 1.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.503). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.162).
After 109 steps the tape spans 37,151 cells (26,993 left of the start, 395 right), with a density of 1s of 0.601.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same run as 1RB1RD_1LC0RE_1LD1LC_1RA0LB_0RD0RF_0RD--- (observed, not proved). At every one of the first 107 steps from blank tape the two machines have the same tape and the head on the same cell. Their tables differ, and no renaming of the states turns one into the other. While they run, the states pair up as A–A, B–B, C–C, D–D, E–B, E–E, F–E, F–F (this machine first), which is not one to one. Transitions not used in these steps: this machine never uses F1 and the other never uses F1. Lean proves (lean/Twin.lean in the other machine's folder, lock_or_break, not_halts_of_noBreak) that the two runs have the same tape, the same head position and paired states up to the first break, a configuration where the paired states act differently, and that neither machine halts if no break ever comes. A halt of either machine is itself a break, and the halting transitions of the two do not correspond, so the two are not known to halt together.

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0LE_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_1LD0RF_0RA---: rename A→B, B→C, C→D, D→A, E→E, F→F; it is this table started in state D
  • 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC---: rename A→D, B→A, C→B, D→C, E→E, F→F and exchange left and right; it is this table started in state B, in a mirror

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

  • 1RB1RE_1RC0RF_0LD---_1LE1LD_1RA0LB_0RE0RF: 8,004,077 configurations, the last at step 8,004,076 here and step 10,000,000 there

summary: A bouncer on the left; on the right a list of runs of 1s separated by 00 whose lengths are 13, 19, 25, 31, ... (13 + 6i), sorted, with multiplicities that fall off from one length to the next (616, 188, 121, 37, 22, 7, 4, 1 at 10^9 steps).
